steps.title: Dark and fruity
steps.body: Pinotage gives deep-coloured wines with red and black fruit: plum, mulberry, cherry and blackberry. Many show smoky, earthy notes, and some a hint of banana or coffee. It's medium to full-bodied, with medium tannin and fairly high alcohol. It is uniquely South African.

steps.title: A deliberate cross
steps.body: In 1925, Professor Abraham Perold, at Stellenbosch University, crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsault, then called Hermitage in South Africa, hence the name. He hoped to combine Pinot's quality with Cinsault's robustness and yield. The first commercial wine was released in 1961. It inherited Cinsault's vigour and Pinot's red fruit.

options: It's a type of Pinot Noir
Cinsault was called Hermitage in South Africa
steps.explanation: Pinot plus Hermitage, the local name for Cinsault, gave Pinotage.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: Look for deep colour and ripe dark fruit with a smoky or earthy edge. Some styles show a sweet, coffee or chocolate note, from heavily toasted oak. Poorly made examples can show acetone or burnt rubber, from volatile compounds, which gave it a bad reputation in the 1990s.

steps.prompt: Pinotage was created by crossing Pinot Noir and Cabernet Sauvignon.
steps.explanation: Not true. Its parents are Pinot Noir and Cinsault.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinotage gives plum, mulberry and smoky notes
It's a 1925 cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault
